items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

items.link_text: 1850 United States Federal Census - Schuylkill County

entry.rationale: Tree records Patrick's birth as ~1845 in Ireland (F1, from the 1850 census), while the question says Pennsylvania; the birthplace is unsettled. The Schuylkill County Church Records collection is name-searchable. Search Patrick Flynn baptism with variants (Flinn, Flin, Patt, Patk) and parents Thomas Flynn (tree: b. ~1818 Ireland) with any wife. A baptism naming both parents is the direct record. loc_001: Catholic registers sit with the Philadelphia diocese, not the county, so also check parish-level registers. If none is found, the Irish birth means the baptism may be outside the US.

Dedicated search for the marriage of candidate father Thomas Flynn to a woman of unknown name. It would confirm the couple as a unit, give her name, and its date relative to ~1845 corroborates Thomas as father. It does not alone prove Patrick is their child. Collections: Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677-1950 and Compiled Marriages 1700-1900 are name-searchable; church marriage registers also. Any surname found is not assumed to be her birth name, since a remarriage is possible. If the marriage was in Ireland it will not appear here.

Patrick's own death (tree F2: 12 Mar 1908, Schuylkill County, cited to S3 Pennsylvania Death Certificates). A baptism may not exist if he was born in Ireland, so this is the route to an origin. Statewide registration began 1906 (loc_001), so a 1908 certificate exists. Pennsylvania Death Certificates 1906-1968 is name-searchable. Read the image for parents' names, birthplace and informant, and re-check what S3 actually recorded.

Patrick's own marriage record(s). Marriage entries often state age, birthplace and sometimes parents' names, which matters because his birth parish is unknown. Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677-1950 and County Marriages 1885-1950 are name-searchable; also church marriages. Witnesses are FAN names, possibly kin.

Requested by the researcher. The 1870 census (Ancestry collection 7163, paid index) can place Patrick, probably grown and perhaps still in Thomas's household or next to him, and gives birthplace and parents' foreign-birth status. Relationship to head is not recorded until 1880, so co-residence alone does not prove parentage. Search Patrick/Thomas Flynn with spelling variants in Schuylkill County first, then statewide. Compare against the 1850 and 1860 households already in the tree (S1, S2). Link: https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7163/

Estate of Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818, so he could die anywhere to about 1900; window set by his lifespan, not Patrick's) and of Patrick (d. 1908). Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683-1994 is browse-only (personCount 0), so browse the Schuylkill Register of Wills images (loc_001). A will or administration naming heirs would name Patrick as son. Also lists FAN names: executors, appraisers, creditors.

FAN item: neighbors and siblings in the Thomas Flynn household and adjoining households across 1850, 1860 and 1880. 1880 records relationship to head, which the tree's 1850 and 1860 sources lack. Siblings found here lead to their own baptisms, marriages and death certificates naming the same parents, testing whether Thomas is the father.

Burial, cemetery and obituary entries for Patrick after his 12 Mar 1908 death: a parish burial register, cemetery stone (Find a Grave) and local newspaper obituary may name a birthplace, age and surviving relatives such as siblings or a father. Neighboring family plots are FAN evidence.

Set collection_url to one of these urls, or leave it off for a site-wide search.

Follow Caroline forward as a married woman; neighbors in 1860 and relationship-to-head in 1880 may show a Voss parent or sibling living with or next to her, and birthplaces of her children's grandparents. Bridges the gap between the 1850 household and her later life.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

items.exhaustive_search_summary: Only the 1850 census (FamilySearch, Ancestry, MyHeritage) has been searched for q_001. Post-1860 censuses, probate, church, and vital records have not yet been searched.
items.narrative_markdown: Patrick Flynn appears in the 1850 census in Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill County household. Co-enumeration is indirect evidence that supports but does not prove parentage. Post-1860 censuses, probate, and church records have not yet been searched.

entry.rationale: Tree and log: the 1850 census places Patrick (age 5) in Thomas Flynn's household, dwelling 84, Schuylkill County; this is co-residence only (ps_001 tier possible) and the 1850 timeline has a 1851-1860 gap. 1860 and 1870 re-test the household; the 1880 schedule is the first to state relationship to head, and a Patrick in a household with Thomas as father would be direct support. Note the tree records birth in Ireland (~1845) while the question says PA; census birthplace entries test that.

Tree fact: death 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County, cited to a Pennsylvania death certificate. Statewide registration began 1906 (loc_001), so this certificate exists; collection 2255317 Pennsylvania Death Certificates 1906-1968 is name-searchable. Check the image for parents' names and birthplace (informant bias applies). Birth is likely in Ireland, so a baptism may not be reachable; the subject's own death entry is the route to origin.

Burial entry, headstone and obituary for Patrick's 1908 death: parish burial registers, cemetery records, Find a Grave and local newspapers often give age, birthplace and surviving relatives (siblings are FAN leads). Own death/burial item since a baptism may not exist for an Irish birth around 1845.

Collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, Schuylkill County Church Records, is name-searchable. loc_001: Catholic registers sit with the Diocese/Archdiocese of Philadelphia and are held at the parish; some coal-region church films are browse-only image groups, so add image browse if the name search underdelivers. Look for baptisms of Flynn siblings naming Thomas and a mother, and Patrick's confirmation or burial. Search variants Flinn, Flin, Flyn, Patt, Pat.

Dedicated item for the marriage of Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818, Ireland per tree) to a wife: it confirms the couple as a unit and may give the mother's name, but only a first marriage gives a maiden name, and no remarriage is excluded, so do not treat any surname found as her birth name. The marriage probably occurred in Ireland or in PA church registers before Patrick's birth; check Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677-1950 and Compiled Marriages 1700-1900 (both name-searchable) plus parish registers. The marriage date alone does not prove Patrick is their child.

Patrick's own marriage (undated, spouse unknown) may name his parents or birthplace in the church or civil entry; County Marriages 1885-1950 is name-searchable and church registers cover earlier years. Marriage entries often state birthplace for Irish immigrants.

Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818) could die anywhere from the 1850s into the 1900s, so the window is sized to his lifespan, not Patrick's. loc_001: the county Register of Wills holds wills and administrations from 1811; collection 1999196 Pennsylvania Probate Records is browse-only (personCount 0), so browse the Schuylkill dockets image by image. A will or administration naming heirs including Patrick would be direct evidence. Also check a possible wife's estate.

FAN item: siblings and neighbors of Patrick (the households near dwelling 84 in 1850, and any Flynn siblings found in sequences 1 and 4). A sibling's death certificate, marriage or obituary naming the same parents tests Patrick's parentage independently and would show whether Thomas's wife was the mother.

Tree gives Thomas Flynn born ~1818 in Ireland, so his arrival and naturalization may state origin and family. loc_001: coal-region naturalization films are browse-only, so browse the Schuylkill court naturalization records image by image; ship manifests from 1845-1850 are a further lead.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.notes: 1870 census: Michael Sheahan, farmer, household outside Schuylkill County. Establishes the 'before' point -- not yet in the coal region and not yet employed in mining.

1882 city/county directory: Michael Sheahan, occupation 'miner', Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. Establishes the 'after' point. Neither record explains the move itself -- found incidentally, not part of any plan.

entry.rationale: Tree and log: 1870 census shows Michael Sheahan a farmer outside Schuylkill County (log_001); an 1882 directory lists him as a miner in Schuylkill County (log_002; tree F2, F3). The 1880 census (United States Census, 1880, name-searchable) falls between and shows whether he was already in the coal region, his occupation, birthplace and household, bracketing the move. Search Sheahan variants (Shehan, Sheehan, Shean, Shahan) in Schuylkill and nationally.

loc_001: Catholic registers stay at parishes under the Archdiocese of Philadelphia; the Schuylkill County Church Records collection is name-searchable. Baptisms of children, marriages and burials place the family in a coal-town parish and date arrival; transfer notes or an origin parish may appear. items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

**Mode:** create. The question is q_001, "Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?". No plan existed for it. The only earlier plan, pl_001, belongs to q_002.

**What the tree already records**
- **Birth:** Patrick's birth is about 1845 in Ireland (F1, cited to the 1850 census). The objective says born in Pennsylvania, which conflicts with this.
- **Death:** 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County (F2, cited to the Pennsylvania death certificate, S3). The tree holds no parent names from it.
- **Father:** Thomas Flynn (I2), born about 1818 in Ireland, is linked as father (R1). The only support is the 1850 census, where Patrick, age 5, is listed in Thomas's household at dwelling 84. That census does not state relationships, so the link is inferred.
- **Mother:** No mother is recorded.
- **Gap:** The timeline flags 1851–1860 as a gap. The 1860 census has not been searched.
- **No pending-hints item:** Patrick has no FamilySearch ark in the tree, so I added no hints-review item.

**Plan pl_002 (active), in execution order**
1. **pli_004:** Patrick's 1908 death certificate, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch. It is name-searchable and should give parents' names and who supplied them.
2. **pli_005:** Census 1860–1880, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch. It tracks the household and reaches 1880, which records relationships.
3. **pli_006:** Patrick's own burial and church entries, 1845–1912, Schuylkill County church records, FamilySearch. A baptism will not exist because he was born in Ireland.
4. **pli_007:** Patrick's own marriage, 1865–1895, Pennsylvania county and civil marriages, FamilySearch. These entries often name parents.
5. **pli_008:** The parents' marriage to each other (Thomas Flynn and Patrick's mother), 1835–1850, in Pennsylvania or Ireland. No maiden name is assumed. The marriage would not by itself prove Patrick is their child.
6. **pli_009:** Probate, 1850–1912, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch. It is browse-only (personCount 0). The window follows Thomas's and Patrick's lifespans.
7. **pli_010:** The family's neighbors and kin (the associates item), 1850–1870, plus church sponsors, to find siblings and the Irish origin.
8. **pli_011:** Naturalization and Philadelphia port records, 1845–1900. The naturalization volumes are browse-only. These records name an Irish home county or town.

The own-death/burial item is pli_006, and the parents' marriage item is pli_008. No item has a fallback relationship. The researcher should note that Ireland is outside the researched locality, so a locality survey for Ireland is needed before pli_008 can search Irish registers.

**Hand-off:** search-records for all eight items, since they are all on FamilySearch.

---

This plan is for finding out who Patrick Flynn's parents were. Records show he was probably born in Ireland around 1845, not in Pennsylvania as first assumed, and that he lived as a child in the household of a Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County. Only the 1850 census puts them together, and that census does not state family relationships, so the plan tests the link. It starts with Patrick's 1908 death certificate, which may name his parents. Next come later censuses, his burial and marriage entries, and the marriage of Thomas and Patrick's mother. After that it looks at wills and estate files, neighbors and relatives, and naturalization and ship records that could name the Irish home town.

Next, the FamilySearch collections named in the plan will be searched in that order, starting with the death certificate.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

| 7 | pli_007 | Probate/municipal | FamilySearch, Málaga | 1845–1905 | Parental estates and municipal records |

items.guide_markdown:
## Vélez-Málaga, Málaga, Spain — 1835-1870

Before civil registration (1871) the parish books are the vital record. Santa María's books from 1837 are on FamilySearch, unindexed but full-text searchable; one births volume for 1841-1845 is name-indexed.

entry.jurisdiction: Santa María parish, Vélez-Málaga, Málaga, Andalusia, Spain
entry.rationale: Tree holds only Birth about 1843 in Vélez-Málaga, no parents, no sources. loc_001: civil registration began 1871, so the parish baptism is the primary record, and entries normally name both parents and the four grandparents. The 1841-1845 births volume (004458370) is 96% name-indexed, so search it by name first, with variants (Josefa/María Josefa, García/Garcia, Romero). Name-searchable collections: Spain, Baptisms, 1502-1940 (1500692) and Spain, Catholic Church Records (1784529). Per Spain Naming Customs, García Romero suggests father García and mother Romero, but that order is unsettled until a record names the parents separately.

entry.jurisdiction: Santa María parish, Vélez-Málaga, Málaga, Andalusia, Spain
entry.rationale: Fallback if item 1 misses: 'about 1843' may be off by years and the indexed volume covers only 1841-1845. The Santa María registers from 1837 (image groups 004104131) are not name-indexed but are full-text searchable, so run a full-text co-occurrence search on García and Romero as separate terms plus Josefa, unscoped, then browse the images of the register years if needed. Also check other Vélez-Málaga parishes if the guide's locality entry lists them.

Dedicated item for the candidate parents' marriage to each other (Spain, Marriages, 1565-1950, name-searchable, plus church marriage registers). It would confirm the couple as a unit, give the mother's maiden name (Spanish women keep their own surname, so a marriage entry usually names her birth surname and her parents), and its date relative to about 1843 corroborates parents otherwise found indirectly. It does not by itself prove María Josefa is their child; the baptism must place her with them. Window set by the parents' likely first marriage before her birth, with a remarriage possible.

Her own marriage entry (Spain, Marriages, 1565-1950, name-searchable; church marriage registers). Marriage entries and any pre-marriage file normally state age, birthplace and both parents' names, and they give a cross-check on the birth year if the baptism is hard to find. Her spouse and place of marriage are unknown in the tree, so search by name across Málaga province.

Her own death or burial entry (Spain, Deaths, 1600-1920 and parish burial registers, name-searchable). The 1837 start of Santa María's registers covers 1843, but the approximate birth year and possible birth in another parish mean a baptism may be missed; death entries typically state age and parents' names. Dated after she was last known alive; under her married status she keeps the surname García Romero.

FAN item: baptisms of possible siblings (children of a García and a Romero in Santa María) and godparents, who are often relatives. A sibling's baptism naming the same parents places the household and tests the surname order; godparents point to the extended family. Window spans likely parental child-bearing years around 1843.

Spain, Málaga, Municipal Records, 1760-1956 (2015362, name-searchable) may hold municipal censuses (padrones), notarial or civil records placing María Josefa in a García Romero household, plus parental wills or estates naming her. Date window sized to the parents' plausible deaths, up to about 60 years after her birth, not to her own life.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1838-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

entry.rationale: Pennsylvania has no civil birth registration before 1906 (loc_001), so baptisms are the primary birth evidence. Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records is name-searchable; search children of John Doyle and Bridget Halloran/Holloran/Halleran/Hallorin. Bridget b. ~1838 Ireland and Ellen married 1865-75 (log_003), so children span roughly 1855-1878 and parish registers name both parents.

United States Census 1860, 1870 and 1880 are name-searchable and name every household member; 1880 also gives relationship. Find the Doyle household with Bridget and Ellen to list siblings, and the 1880 Kearney household for Doyle stepchildren. Log_002 (1900) records 9 born, 2 living, so many children may have died before any census; check Doyle variants (Doyl, Doyl, Hallaran).

Dedicated search for John Doyle and Bridget Halloran's marriage to each other, in Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages 1677-1950 and Compiled Marriages 1700-1900 (both name-searchable), plus church marriage entries. Establishes the couple as a unit, the marriage date (bounding the first child's birth), and possibly a home parish. Does not itself prove any child; the marriage was before Ellen's (1865-75, log_003).

Marriages of the Doyle children, which name parents (as Ellen's does, log_003). Pennsylvania, County Marriages 1885-1950 and Civil Marriages 1677-1950 are name-searchable; search brides/grooms surnamed Doyle with parents John and Bridget. Covers the 2 surviving children plus any who married and died before 1900.

John Doyle's own death or burial entry (he died before Bridget's 1879 remarriage to Martin Kearney, log_001), likely in a Catholic parish register or cemetery. Burial entries of Doyle infants and children would also identify the 7 deceased children. Search church records name-searchable first; volume 007936751 (church records 1842-1895) is browse-only (personCount 0 / 0% searchable) so browse it image by image if the name search fails.

Estate of John Doyle (died before 1879) and of Bridget (alive 1900, death after), held by the Register of Wills from 1811 (loc_001). Pennsylvania, Probate Records 1683-1994 is browse-only (personCount 0), as is probate volume 007936749 (1851-1930); browse the Schuylkill volumes. Administration papers or a will name heirs; window runs to 1930 because Bridget's own probate may postdate 1900.

Pennsylvania, Death Certificates 1906-1968 is name-searchable. Death certificates of Ellen and the other survivor, and of Bridget herself, give parents' names and possibly informant siblings. Bridget b. ~1838 may have died after 1906.

FAN and non-FamilySearch coverage: obituaries (Pottsville and coal-region newspapers), cemetery listings and Find a Grave for Doyle, Kearney and Halloran burials; Martin Kearney's household and Bridget's Halloran siblings could name Doyle nieces, nephews and stepchildren. Also check the 1900 Kearney household neighbors and the Kearney stepchildren's records for the second surviving child.

John Doyle may have served in the Civil War (an Irish coal-region man dying before 1879); United States Civil War Soldiers Index 1861-1865 is name-searchable. Widow's pension files name minor children with birth dates. Pension index lead only; Doyle is a common name so verify identity against Bridget.

## Stagstrup Sogn, Thisted Amt, Denmark - late 1700s

For a male subject born 1779, two record classes carry parentage. Church books (kirkeboeger) hold the baptism naming both parents. The military levy rolls (laegdsruller), kept from 1789, enroll every boy under his father's name from childhood - direct evidence of the father. Danish patronymics (Nielsen = son of Niels) point to the father's given name but not the specific man. The Stagstrup register is only ~3% indexed, so plan to browse images.

Patronymic Nielsen implies father's given name Niels, but that does not identify which Niels. Try spelling variants (Mikkel/Michael/Mikkal, Blyeberg/Bly-/Bleeberg).

Per loc_001 and the Denmark Military Records wiki page, levying rolls from 1788/89 list all males from birth under the father's name, direct parentage evidence for a son. FAN item: baptisms of Mikkel's siblings in the same register, and the godparents (faddere) named at each baptism, who are often kin of the parents. Shows the family unit under a single Niels and supplies names for probate and census matching.

Denmark Census 1787-1930 (1403625 not used; collection 2078555 irrelevant) - search the 1787 and 1801 censuses, which name every household member with age and relationship, to find a Niels with a son Mikkel of about 8 (1787) or 22 (1801) or about 1 month old near Stagstrup. items.guide_markdown:
## Muhlenberg County, Kentucky — c. 1870-1890

Statewide death certificates begin 1911; no certificate can cover a death in the 1870s-1880s. County death registers (1804888) exist but the 1860s-1870s coverage is partial. For this era, **probate records are the primary death evidence**: administrator bonds name the widow or heir, estate settlements are dated, and register entries bracket the death within months. Muhlenberg County probate (1875188) survives well for the 1870s and is browse-only. Supplement with church burials, cemetery records, and census bracketing.

entry.rationale: Review pending FamilySearch hints on ZZWK-EL1 before searching — an attached hint may already answer the question.

The question presupposes death certificates. Tree records Elijah's birth c. 1814 and last residence 1870 in Muhlenberg County; loc_001 says statewide certificates begin 1 Jan 1911, so a certificate could exist only if he lived past age 97. Kentucky Deaths, 1911-1967 is name-searchable: run it with variant spellings (Wilkins, Wilkens, Wilkin) as a quick test to rule a certificate in or out and to exclude a younger namesake. A certificate, if found, gives date, place, age, parents and informant.

Because no certificate can cover an 1870s-1890s death, county death registers are the nearest substitute. Kentucky, Deaths and Burials, 1843-1970 is name-searchable; loc_001 warns 1860s-1870s coverage is partial and many counties lack surviving registers, so a miss is not proof. Search with name variants, Muhlenberg and adjoining counties.

Per loc_001, probate is the primary death evidence for this era and Muhlenberg probate survives well for the 1870s. Kentucky Probate Records, 1727-1990 is browse-only (personCount 0), so browse the county's will books, administrator bonds, inventories and settlements. Window is sized to the decedent's death (after 1870, to a settlement filed years later), not the 1870 census. Will or bond brackets the death within months and names heirs.

Tree records only the 1870 Muhlenberg residence, the last known alive date. The 1880 census gives relationship to head and, if Elijah (about 66) is absent or his wife is listed widowed, brackets death to 1870-1880. Search by name variants and in the households of likely adult children.

FAN item: Kentucky, County Marriages, 1797-1954 is name-searchable. Marriage returns of Wilkins children or a widow's remarriage in Muhlenberg often state the father as deceased or give consent by a parent, bracketing Elijah's death and identifying family to trace in the probate item.

Per loc_001, church burial registers and cemetery records can also bracket the death. Search Find a Grave and county cemetery surveys and church minute books for an Elijah Wilkins with birth c. 1814; a stone gives death date and burial place. Confirm identity against the 1870 household before accepting.

Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1840-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

entry.rationale: Review pending FamilySearch hints on ZZKR-TH2 before searching — an attached hint may already answer the question.

The FamilySearch tree (not the project tree) attaches a christening for Thomas on 14 Mar 1842 at St. Patrick's Church, Pottsville, and lists Patrick Kerrigan (b. abt 1815 Mayo, d. 1880 Pottsville) and Mary Gallagher (b. abt 1818 Ireland) as parents. Treat these as leads, not facts: read the baptism entry itself for parents' names and sponsors. The Schuylkill church collection is name-searchable; the register is held by the parish/Archdiocese of Philadelphia (loc_001), so check the image for the original wording. Try spellings Kerrigan/Kerrican/Kerigan/Carrigan/Kernan.

Dedicated search for the candidate parents' marriage to each other (Patrick Kerrigan and Mary Gallagher, a lead from the FamilySearch tree). It would confirm them as a couple, supply the mother's maiden name only if this was her first marriage (not assumed; Gallagher could be a prior married name), and its date relative to the 1842 birth corroborates parentage but does not by itself prove Thomas is their child. They may have married in Ireland (Mayo) before emigrating, so search Pennsylvania civil marriages and Catholic church marriage registers (both name-searchable), and note that Irish civil registration does not cover this period. A companion item (sibling baptisms, probate) tests Mary's surname.

The FamilySearch tree attaches the 1850 census for Pottsville to Thomas. 1850 names every household member with age and birthplace, but gives no relationship to head, so a child aged about 8 living with Patrick and Mary is consistent with, not proof of, parentage. Read the household for siblings and neighbours (FAN) and birthplace of each parent.

The 1860, 1870 and 1880 censuses (all name-searchable) track the candidate household forward; 1880 records relationship to head, and would show Thomas's own household (wife Ellen Burke, daughter Bridget b. 1871) and any Kerrigan parent living with or near him. Patrick is said to have died in 1880, so the 1880 schedule may catch him or Mary as a widow.

Estate file of Patrick Kerrigan, said to have died 1880 in Pottsville; window set by the parent's lifespan (and Mary's possible later death), not Thomas's. The Pennsylvania probate collection is browse-only (personCount 0), so this is an image browse of the Schuylkill Register of Wills, with a will or administration naming Thomas as son as direct evidence. Statewide death registration begins only in 1906 (loc_001), so probate substitutes for a death record.

FAN/sibling item: baptisms of other Kerrigan children born to Patrick and Mary in Pottsville parishes, and sponsors on them, plus marriages of Thomas's siblings. Records of this kind that name the same parents place Thomas in the family and test whether Gallagher was Mary's own surname. Name-searchable church collection; use variant spellings.

Thomas's own death (1898, Pottsville) pre-dates statewide registration, so look to the subject's burial entry in Catholic parish registers, cemetery records and newspaper obituaries for Pottsville. Obituaries and burial entries may name surviving parents or siblings, and family burial plots may group Patrick and Mary with Thomas. Also covers Patrick's 1880 burial.

Thomas was aged about 19-23 during the Civil War; the Civil War Soldiers Index is name-searchable and could lead to service or pension files that name a parent as dependent. Speculative but cheap, and ranks last because it only helps if he served.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.
